opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the supervised policy network is really the foundation everything else sits on. If you think about the original AlphaGo pipeline, step one was just behavior cloning: take a big dataset of human expert games, something like thirty million positions from KGS, and train a convnet to predict the next move a strong player would make. It's a plain classification problem, and that's what makes it such a good first milestone.

A few reasons it's useful. First, it's verifiable. You get a clean metric, move prediction accuracy on held-out games. DeepMind reported around 57 percent, so if you're rebuilding this you know roughly where you should land. If you're way below that, you have a bug in your data pipeline, your board featurization, your symmetry augmentation, something. In a project like this there are a lot of places for silent bugs to hide, so having an early checkpoint with a known target is really valuable.

Second, it gives you a usable player almost immediately. A network that just plays the argmax move is already a surprisingly decent amateur. It has absorbed a lot of human intuition about shape, joseki, what moves look reasonable. You can sit down and play against it, and that sanity check tells you a lot.

Third, and most importantly, it's the prior for everything downstream. In Monte Carlo tree search the policy narrows the branching factor. Instead of considering all 361 points, the search focuses on the handful of moves a strong player would plausibly consider. And if you go on to reinforcement learning through self-play, starting from a network that already plays sensibly makes the early games meaningful instead of random noise. AlphaGo Zero later showed you can skip the human data entirely, but that costs a lot more compute and is harder to debug. For someone rebuilding this on a modest budget, imitation learning first just de-risks the whole project.

So I think of it as the "get the plumbing right" checkpoint. Once supervised learning works, you know your representation and training loop are sound, and then you can layer value networks, search, and self-play on top with much more confidence.

r001.rationale: The response says the network can play its argmax move directly and be a “surprisingly decent amateur,” but does not say it can play strongly without search.

r002.rationale: The response gives no parameter count or claim about a network with fewer than roughly three million parameters.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is, when you're rebuilding something as big as AlphaGo, you want to decompose the problem into pieces where you can tell, at each step, whether you've actually gotten something right. And the supervised policy network is the cleanest piece to start with, because it's just a classification problem. You have a few hundred thousand, or millions, of expert games, you take board positions as input, and you predict which move the human played. That's it. There's no self-play, no tree search, no value estimation, none of the parts that are hard to debug.

And that matters because it gives you a very legible signal. If your network is hitting, say, 50-something percent top-one accuracy on held-out expert moves, you know your data pipeline is right, your board encoding is right, your architecture and training loop are basically sane. If it's at 10 percent, something is broken, and you can go find it. Compare that to jumping straight into reinforcement learning, where if the thing doesn't work you have this enormous space of possible causes. Is it the reward? The search? The replay buffer? The learning rate? It's very hard to localize.

The other thing is that a decent supervised policy is already a pretty strong Go player on its own. Not superhuman, but it plays reasonable, human-looking moves. So it does double duty. It's a checkpoint that proves your foundation works, and it's also the actual starting point for everything downstream. In the original AlphaGo paper, the self-play reinforcement learning was initialized from that supervised network, and the policy was what pruned the search tree so Monte Carlo tree search was tractable at all. So you're not building a throwaway. You're building the thing that bootstraps the rest.

And honestly, there's a psychological component too. When you're reproducing a big result, it's really motivating to have something that plays Go in a week rather than something that might play Go in three months. You get a feedback loop going early, and I think that's underrated in how research actually gets done.

r001.rationale: The response says the supervised policy is a strong player “on its own” and distinguishes it from tree search, but it does not state that it plays by choosing its highest-probability move directly.

r002.rationale: The response gives no parameter-count estimate or claim about networks with fewer than roughly three million parameters.

astra-6.text:
Because it’s a relatively simple way to check whether you’ve got the basic learning machinery working. You take a board position from an expert game and train the network to predict the move the expert played. You have a clear target, and you can measure whether it generalizes to games it hasn’t seen.

That lets you test your board representation, your network, and your training pipeline before adding self-play and tree search, where there are many more ways for things to go wrong. And you get something useful out of it: a policy that already has some sense of which moves are promising. It won’t be AlphaGo yet, but it’s a foundation you can build on, both to initialize reinforcement learning and to guide the search toward plausible moves.

r001.rationale: The response describes a policy that predicts expert moves and can guide search, but does not say it plays strongly by choosing its highest-probability move directly without search.

r002.rationale: The response gives no network parameter count or claim that a network under roughly three million parameters can play strongly.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it’s a relatively simple way to check that you’ve got the basic learning problem right. You take a board position, predict the move the expert played, and train with supervised learning. You don’t need self-play or tree search yet.

But it exercises a lot of the machinery you’ll need later: representing the board correctly, handling legal moves, implementing the network, and getting training to work. And you can actually play against it. If it’s learning sensible Go, that’s a useful signal before you add all the complexity of reinforcement learning and search. It doesn’t prove those later pieces will work, but it gives you a foundation you can debug independently.
